blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conductors

  • Those substance that allow the flow of electric current.
  • Common examples include metals like copper and aluminum.
Conductors are broadly classified in two types

(A) Metallic conductors - conduct electricity trough the movement of electrons & and no chemical change occur

Example: Metals like Copper, Aluminum etc.

(B) Electrolytic conductors - conduct electricity through the movement of ions in solution or molten state & involve chemical changes during conduction.

Electrolytic conductor classified based on extent of ionization in water as strong & weak electrolytes

• Strong electrolytes -
 completely dissociate in aqueous solution

Example: Salts, strong acids and strong bases in water

Salt   -   NaCl, KCl  etc.

Strong Acid -  HCl, $H_2SO_4$ ,  HBr etc.

Strong Base - NaOH, KOH etc.

• Weak electrolytes - partially dissociate in aqueous solution

Example:  $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$,$\text{HCN}$,$\text{NH}_3$, etc.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Conductance (G)

$G=\frac{1}{R}$

Explanation: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in Siemens.

• Specific resistance/Resistivity ($\rho$)

$R = \rho l/\ A$

$\ell = 1\ \text{cm}, \ A = 1\ \text{cm}^2, \ \text{therefore} \ \rho = R$

$\therefore V = A \times \ell = 1\ \text{cm}^3$

$\text{Unit of } \rho \rightarrow \Omega \cdot \text{cm}$

• Specific conductance/ Conductivity (k(kappa) :-

It is defined as the reciprocal of specific resistance,

$ k = \frac{1}{\rho} $

𝜅 = 𝐺 × 𝐺*

Specific conductance = Conductance × Cell constant

Hence specific conductivity of a solution is defined as the conductance offered by 1 $cm^3$of electrolytic solution.

$\ \text{Unit of } k = \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}\ (S × \text{cm}^{-1})$

• Cell constant

G*= l/A

• Molar conductivity or Molar conductance
 $(\Lambda_m \text{ or } \lambda_m)$

$\Lambda_m = k \times V$

$\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$

$\text{Unit} \rightarrow \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^2 \, \text{mol}^{-1}$($ \text{S } \text{cm}^2 \, \text{mol}^{-1}$)

• Relation between $\Lambda_{\text{eq}} \quad \text{and} \quad \Lambda_m$

$\Lambda_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\Lambda_m}{V_f}$

blocks.title: Factors Affecting Electrolytic Conductance
blocks.text:
• Inter ionic attraction
    • Polarity of solvent
    • Viscosity of medium
    • Temperature
    • Hydrated size
    • Dilution

• On increasing the dilution conductance (G) increases. For a strong electrolyte, on dilution, interionic force of attraction decreases, therefore, conductance increases. For a weak electrolyte, on dilution, degree of dissociation (α) increases, therefore, conductance increases.
    • On dilution, specific conductance decreases because number of ions in 1 ml solution decreases.
    • On dilution, equivalent and molar conductance increases because normality and molarity decrease.

blocks.title: Data
blocks.text:
• Constants and Definitions:
  • Acronym for Electrolytes: SAB (Salts, Acids, Bases).
  • Strong Electrolytes: Example includes NaCl, which completely dissociates.
  • Weak Electrolytes: Example includes CH₃COOH, which partially dissociates.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Conductors: Confusing them with insulators, which do not allow electric flow.
  • Electrolytes: Assuming all ionic compounds are strong electrolytes without considering solubility and dissociation.
Note: Mastery of the flow of ions and electrons is crucial for understanding conductors and electrolytes.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: The resistance of a 1N solution of salt is $50 \, \Omega,$ Calculate the equivalent conductance of the solution, if the two platinum electrodes in solution are 2.1 cm apart and each having an area of 4.2 $\text{cm}^2$.
blocks.answer:
Step 1: Calculate Conductance

$G = \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{50} = 0.02 \, \Omega^{-1}$

Step 2: Calculate Conductivity κ

$\kappa = G \cdot \frac{d}{A} = 0.02 \cdot \frac{2.1}{4.2} = 0.02 \cdot 0.5 = 0.01 \, \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}$

$\text{Step 3: Calculate Equivalent Conductance } \Lambda_{\text{eq}}$

$\text{Since } C = 1 \, \text{mol/L}$

$\Lambda_{\text{eq}} = \kappa \cdot \frac{1000}{C} = 0.01 \cdot \frac{1000}{1} = 10 \, \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^2 \, \text{mol}^{-1}$

modules.name: Molar Conductance of Electrolytes at Infinite Dilution

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Determination of Molar Conductance of Electrolytes at Infinite Dilution$\text{ } (\Lambda_m^{\infty} \text{ or } \Lambda_m^0)$

Debye Huckel Onsager equation

$\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\infty} - A\sqrt{C}
 \quad \text{}$$$

$\Lambda_m$= molar conductance at concentration C,

$ \Lambda_m^{\infty}$= molar conductance at infinite dilution

A =constant and its value is same for a particular type of electrolyte.

blocks.title: Kohlrausch’s Law of Independent Migration of Ions
blocks.text:
At infinite dilution, when dissociation of electrolyte is complete; each ion makes a definite contribution towards equivalent conductivity of any electrolyte irrespective of the nature of other ion associated with it. This law states that the equivalent conductivity of any electrolyte at infinite dilution $\Lambda_{eq}^{\infty}$is the sum of equivalent ionic conductivities of the cation and anion given by the electrolytes at infinite dilution.

Applications of Kohlrausch's Law

  • To calculate conductance of weak electrolyte.
  • To calculate degree of dissociation
  • To calculate dissociation constant of weak electrolyte
  • To calculate Solubility (s) and Solubility product $K_{SP}$ for sparingly soluble salts.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• The sum of equivalent ionic conductivities of the cation and anion given by the electrolytes at infinite dilution.

$\Lambda_{eq}^{\infty} = \Lambda_c^{\infty }  + \Lambda_a^{\infty}$

$\Lambda_c^{\infty }=$Equivalent conductance of a cation at infinite dilution.

$ \Lambda_a^{\infty}=$equivalent conductance of an anion at infinite dilution

• Degree of dissociation

$\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{\text{eq}}}{\Lambda_{\text{eq}}^{\infty}}$  or  $\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{\text{m}}}{\Lambda_{\text{m}}^{\infty}}$

• Calculate the dissociation constant of a weak electrolyte

$K_a=C \alpha^2 /(1 - \alpha)$

$\text{If } \alpha \leq 0.5, \text{ then } K_a = C \alpha^2$

• Calculate the Solubility (s) and $K_{SP}$ of a sparingly soluble salt

$\Lambda_m= \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$

M= s (SOLUBILITY)

$\Lambda_m^{\infty} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{s}$

blocks.text:
• Confusing Resistance and Resistivity: Resistivity $(\rho)$ is a material specific, it tell us how good a material is at resisting current.
Whereas Resistance (R) is actual measurable opposition in specific object made from material

  • Misapplication of Ohm's Law: Ensure conditions like temperature constancy are met before applying.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electrochemical Cells:

  • Devices that convert chemical energy to electrical energy or vice versa.
  • Consists of two electrodes in separate half-cells connected by a salt bridge.
Electrode Potentials:

  • A potential difference indicates a species' tendency to gain or lose electrons.

blocks.title: Electrode Potential
blocks.text:
• Electrode potential - The potential developed between metal electrode and its ions in solution is known as electrode potential.

• The potential developed between metal electrodes and the solution of its ions at 1 M concentration at 1 bar pressure and 298 K is known as standard electrode potential
There are two types of electrode potential: -

• Oxidation Potential (O.P.)

The electrode potential for oxidation half-reaction

$M(s) \rightarrow \text{M}^{n+}(\text{aq}) + n\text{e}^- ;\quad E_{\text{M/M}^{n+}} = \text{O.P.}$

• Tendency to get oxidized.

• Greater the O.P. greater will be the tendency to get oxidized.

• Reduction Potential (R.P.)

• The electrode potential for reduction half-reaction

$\text{M}^{n+}(\text{aq}) + n\text{e}^- \rightarrow M(s) ;\quad E_{\text{M}^{n+}/\text{M}} = \text{R.P.}$

• Tendency to get reduced.
    • Pressure and temperature conditions

• Reference Electrode:

• Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)
For SHE electrode potential is arbitrarily assumed to be zero.

SHE = SOP = –SRP = 0, for SHE. half-reaction

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Standard Electrode Potential ($E^\circ$):

  • Tendency of a chemical species to be reduced, measured under standard conditions.
  • Formula: $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ=E_{\text{cathode}}^\circ-E_{\text{anode}}^\circ$  in reduction potential

blocks.question:
Calculate the standard cell potential for a galvanic cell with the following half-reactions:

  • $Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu$ ($E^\circ = +0.34 \, V$)
  • $Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Zn$ ($E^\circ = -0.76 \, V$)

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Write cell representation for the following redox reaction

$\text{Sn}^{2+} (\text{aq}) + 2\ \text{Ag}^+ (\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} (\text{aq}) + 2\ \text{Ag} (\text{s})$
blocks.answer:
The cell consists of a platinum wire anode dipped in $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ solution and a silver cathode dipped in $\text{Ag}^{+}$ solution, therefore,

$\text{Pt(s)} \mid \text{Sn}^{2+} (\text{aq}), \text{Sn}^{4+} (\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^+ (\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misidentifying the anode and cathode:
  • Anode is where oxidation occurs; Cathode is where reduction occurs.
  • Confusing cell notation:
  • Write anode on the left and cathode on the right in cell notation.

blocks.title: Additional Guidelines
blocks.text:
• Use the mnemonics to aid memorization:
Mnemonic 1: "LEO the lion says GER" - Loss of Electrons is Oxidation; Gain of Electrons is Reduction.

Mnemonic 2: "AN OX and a RED CAT" - Anode is Oxidation; Reduction occurs at the Cathode.

blocks.title: Applications of Electrochemical Series
blocks.text:
• Oxidizing and reducing power –

$\text{Oxidizing power} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SOP}} \\ \text{Reducing power} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SRP}}$

• Reactivity of metals

$\text{Reactivity of metal } \propto {\text{SOP}} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SRP}}$

•   In ECS, the reactivity of metal decreases from top to bottom.

•   Li is the most reactive metal.

• Reactivity of non-metals

$\text{Reactivity of non-metal}  \propto \text{SRP} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SOP}}$

•   In ECS, the reactivity of non-metal increases from top to bottom.

•   $F_2$ is the most reactive non-metal.

• Displacement reactions in solution

More reactive metal / non-metal displaces less reactive metal / non-metal from their solution

$\text{Cu} + 2\ \text{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3\text{)}_2 + 2\ \text{Ag}$

$\text{Ag} + \text{Cu(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

$2\ \text{KI} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\ \text{KCl} + \text{I}_2$

$\text{I}_2 + 2\ \text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

• Metal above hydrogen displaces $\text{H}_2$ from dilute acid solution.

$\text{Zn} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{H}_2(\text{g})$

$\text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{dilute}) \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

blocks.title: Galvanic Cell
blocks.text:
• It has two half–cells, each having a beaker containing a metal strip that dips in its aqueous salt solution
    • The metal strips are called electrodes and are connected by a conducting wire.
    • Two solutions are connected by salt bridge.
    • The oxidation and reduction half reactions occur at separate electrodes and electric current flows through the wire.

Salt Bridge and its functions

• Salt bridge is inverted U-tube containing solution of inert electrolyte with agar-agar or gelatin to convert into semi solid form.

• Ions of inert electrolyte do not involve in any chemical change.

The electrolyte in salt bridge should be such that speed of its cation is nearly equal to speed of its anion. Ex. KCl, $KNO_3$, $NH_4NO_3$

• If $Ag^+$, $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$,$\text{Pb}^{2+}$, $\text{Tl}^+$ ions are present in a cell then KCl is not used because there can be formation of precipitate of AgCl, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ $\text{PbCl}_2$  or TlCl.

Functions

• It connects the solution of two half cells to complete the circuit.
    • It maintains the electrical neutrality of the solution in order to give continuous flow or generation of current.
    • If the salt bridge is removed then voltage drops to zero.
    • It prevents the liquid -liquid junction potential. The potential difference which arises between two solutions when they are brought in contact with each other.

Cell Representation:

$\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{ZnSO}_4(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{CuSO}_4(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Cu(s)}$

Anode                        II                Cathode

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
Which of the following pairs of metals is correctly ordered based on their reducing power?
(a) Al > Zn
(b) Cu > Fe
(c) Au > Ag
(d) Mg > Na
blocks.answer:
Answer: (a) Al > Zn
Explanation: Aluminum has a more negative standard electrode potential than zinc, making it a stronger reducing agent.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Nernst Equation:

  • Relates the cell potential to its standard electrode potential and reaction quotient(Q).
  • Essential for understanding electrochemical cells under non-standard conditions.
Cell EMF (Electromotive Force):

  • The potential difference between two electrodes in an electrochemical cell.
  • Determines the cell's ability to drive an electric current.

blocks.title: Nernst Equation
blocks.text:
It gives relation between electrode potential/ EMF of cell and concentration of electrolytic solution. Walther Nernst derived a relation between free energy change  $ \Delta G^\circ $ and Reaction quotient (Q).

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT \ln Q$

where   $\Delta G$ and $ \Delta G^\circ $are free energy change and standard free energy change; ‘Q’ is reaction quotient.

$-\Delta G = nFE$;  $-\Delta G^\circ = nFE^\circ$

blocks.title: Applications of Nernst Equation and Golden key point
blocks.text:
Applications of Nernst Equation:

• Calculation of electrode potential (ERP or EOP)
    • Calculation of electrode potential and pH or hydrogen electrode
    • Calculation of EMF of cell ($E_{cell}$)

• Prediction and feasibility of a cell reaction
    • Calculation of equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) and $\Delta G^\circ $

Golden Key Point:

• The value of electrode potential does not depend on stoichiometry of half reactions as it is an intensive property.
    • Gibb's free energy is an extensive property.
    • In an electrolytic cell, cathode is negative terminal whereas in Galvanic cell cathode is a positive terminal.
    • Cell reaction is spontaneous, if

$\Delta G$ = – ve        or      $E_{\text{cell}} = +\text{ve}$

• Cell reaction will be in equilibrium, if

$\Delta G$ = 0           or     $-nFE_{\text{cell}}  $= 0 or $E_{\text{cell}} $ = 0

• Work done by a cell:

Let 'n' faraday charge be taken out of a cell of EMF 'E' ; then work done by the cell will be calculated as:

Work = Charge × Potential = nF × E

Work done by cell = Decrease in free energy

-$\Delta G = -nFE \quad \text{or} \quad W_{\text{max}} = +nFE^\circ$

where E° is standard EMF of the cell.

blocks.title: Formulas and mathematics relations
blocks.text:
Nernst Equation:

$E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF} \ln Q$

where, $E$: Cell potential under non-standard conditions

$E^\circ$: Standard cell potential

$R$: Universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K)

$T$: Temperature in Kelvin

$n$: Number of moles of electrons transferred

$F$: Faraday's constant (96485 C/mol)

$Q$: Reaction quotient

Simplified at 25°C (298 K):

$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$

$E = E_0 - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log \frac{[P]}{[R]}$

In general, for a redox cell reaction involving the transfer of n electrons

$aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$

$E_{\text{Cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ignoring Temperature:
  • Assuming the Nernst equation is the same at all temperatures can lead to errors.
  • The $0.0591$ factor is valid only at 25°C.
  • Misidentifying Reaction Quotient (Q):
  • Confusing $Q$ with equilibrium constant $K$, which applies only at equilibrium.
These notes are designed to help you quickly recall the essential points of the Nernst Equation and Cell EMF for efficient revision and application in NEET exams.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
1. Calculate the EMF of the cell

$\text{Cr} \, | \, \text{Cr}^{3+} \, (0.1 \, \text{M}) \, || \, \text{Fe}^{2+} \, (0.01 \, \text{M}) \, | \, \text{Fe}$

(Given)

$E^\circ_{\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}} = -0.75 \, \text{V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = -0.45 \, \text{V}$
blocks.answer:
Half cell reactions are –

At Anode :   $\left[ \text{Cr} \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+} + 3e^- \right] \times 2$

At Cathode   $\left[ \text{Fe}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe} \right] \times 3$

Cell reaction

$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = (\text{SRP})_\text{C} - (\text{SRP})_\text{A} = (-0.45) + (0.75) = 0$.30V

$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\text{Product}]}{[\text{Reactant}]}$

$0.30 - \frac{0.059}{6} \log \frac{[0.1]^2}{[0.01]^3} = 0.30 + \frac{0.24}{6} = 0.34 \, \text{V}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Electrolysis: The process of chemical decomposition of an electrolyte by the passage of electricity is called as electrolysis or electrolytic dissociation. It is carried out in an electrolytic cell where electrical energy is converted into chemical energy
  • Faraday's Laws
First law of electrolysis: Amount of substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to amount of charge passed through the solution

Second Law: When same amount of charge is passed through different electrolyte solutions connected in series then weight of substances deposited or liberated at electrodes are in ratio of their respective equivalent weights

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Faraday's First Law:
$W = Z.Q$

$\mathrm{W}=\frac{\mathrm{E} . \mathrm{I} . \mathrm{t}}{96500}$

$\mathrm{E}=\frac{\text { mol. } \mathrm{wt}}{\mathrm{n}-\text { factor }}$

Variables:

$W$ : mass of substance deposited (in gm)

$Q$ : total charge passed = I × t

Z : Electrochemical equivalent

E : Equivalent weight

I : Current (in Ampere )

t : time (in second)

96500 : Faraday's constant F

Assumptions: Simple ionic substances, 100% efficiency.

  • Faraday's Second Law:
$\mathrm{W}=\frac{\mathrm{E} . \mathrm{I} . \mathrm{t}}{96500}$

if I and t is contant(Constant current for same time) then

W ∝ E

$\frac{W_1}{E_1} = \frac{W_2}{E_2}$

blocks.title: Corrosion
blocks.text:
• In corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons to oxygen and forms metal oxide. Corrosion of iron(which is commonly known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and oxygen (air). Although the chemistry of corrosion is complex but it is understood that at one spot of an iron object oxidation occurs and that spot behaves as an anode.

• Anode:

$\text{Fe(s)} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+} \, (\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^{-}$  ( $E^0Fe^{2+}$/Fe  = -0.44V )

Electrons released at anode move through the metal and go to another spot on the metal and reduce the oxygen in presence of $H^+$ ions (which is believed to be available from H₂CO₃ formed due to dissolution of  $CO_2$ in water). This spot works as a cathode :

• Cathode:

$\text{O}_2 \, (\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+ \, (\text{aq}) + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \, (\ell)$  ( $E^0$ = 1.23 V)

The overall reaction of the miniature cell is the sum of the cathode and anode reactions as follows :

$4\text{Fe}^{2+} \, (\text{aq}) + \text{O}_2 \, (\text{g}) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \, (\ell) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \, (\text{s}) + 8\text{H}^+$

• Prevention From Corrosion

Galvanised iron. Cathodic protection of iron in contact with zinc is provided by galvanization

Cathodic protection by connecting a block of magnesium to an iron pipe buried underground.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
Q. Which of the following conditions does not favor corrosion of iron?

  • Presence of water and air
  • Presence of acidic medium
  • Contact with less reactive metal like copper
  • Coating with zinc (galvanization)
blocks.answer:
Answer (4) Coating with zinc (galvanization)

  • Explanation:
Corrosion of iron is an electrochemical process that requires moisture (water) and oxygen. Acidic conditions increase corrosion. When iron is in contact with a less reactive metal like copper, iron becomes the anode and corrodes faster.
But when coated with zinc (more reactive than iron), zinc corrodes first and protects iron — this is called galvanization.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conductors

  • Those substance that allow the flow of electric current.
  • Common examples include metals like copper and aluminum.
Conductors are broadly classified in two types

(A) Metallic conductors - conduct electricity trough the movement of electrons & and no chemical change occur

Example: Metals like Copper, Aluminum etc.

(B) Electrolytic conductors - conduct electricity through the movement of ions in solution or molten state & involve chemical changes during conduction.

Electrolytic conductor classified based on extent of ionization in water as strong & weak electrolytes

• Strong electrolytes -
 completely dissociate in aqueous solution

Example: Salts, strong acids and strong bases in water

Salt   -   NaCl, KCl  etc.

Strong Acid -  HCl, $H_2SO_4$ ,  HBr etc.

Strong Base - NaOH, KOH etc.

• Weak electrolytes - partially dissociate in aqueous solution

Example:  $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$,$\text{HCN}$,$\text{NH}_3$, etc.

blocks.title: Factors Affecting Electrolytic Conductance
blocks.text:
• Inter ionic attraction
    • Polarity of solvent
    • Viscosity of medium
    • Temperature
    • Hydrated size
    • Dilution

• On increasing the dilution conductance (G) increases. For a strong electrolyte, on dilution, interionic force of attraction decreases, therefore, conductance increases. For a weak electrolyte, on dilution, degree of dissociation (α) increases, therefore, conductance increases.
    • On dilution, specific conductance decreases because number of ions in 1 ml solution decreases.
    • On dilution, equivalent and molar conductance increases because normality and molarity decrease.

blocks.title: Data
blocks.text:
• Constants and Definitions:
  • Acronym for Electrolytes: SAB (Salts, Acids, Bases).
  • Strong Electrolytes: Example includes NaCl, which completely dissociates.
  • Weak Electrolytes: Example includes CH₃COOH, which partially dissociates.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electrochemical Cells:

  • Devices that convert chemical energy to electrical energy or vice versa.
  • Consists of two electrodes in separate half-cells connected by a salt bridge.
Electrode Potentials:

  • A potential difference indicates a species' tendency to gain or lose electrons.

blocks.title: Applications of Electrochemical Series
blocks.text:
• Oxidizing and reducing power –

$\text{Oxidizing power} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SOP}} \\ \text{Reducing power} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SRP}}$

• Reactivity of metals

$\text{Reactivity of metal } \propto {\text{SOP}} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SRP}}$

•   In ECS, the reactivity of metal decreases from top to bottom.

•   Li is the most reactive metal.

• Reactivity of non-metals

$\text{Reactivity of non-metal}  \propto \text{SRP} \propto \frac{1}{\text{SOP}}$

•   In ECS, the reactivity of non-metal increases from top to bottom.

•   $F_2$ is the most reactive non-metal.

• Displacement reactions in solution

More reactive metal / non-metal displaces less reactive metal / non-metal from their solution

$\text{Cu} + 2\ \text{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3\text{)}_2 + 2\ \text{Ag}$

$\text{Ag} + \text{Cu(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

$2\ \text{KI} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\ \text{KCl} + \text{I}_2$

$\text{I}_2 + 2\ \text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

• Metal above hydrogen displaces $\text{H}_2$ from dilute acid solution.

$\text{Zn} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{H}_2(\text{g})$

$\text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{dilute}) \rightarrow \text{No reaction}$

blocks.title: Galvanic Cell
blocks.text:
• It has two half–cells, each having a beaker containing a metal strip that dips in its aqueous salt solution
    • The metal strips are called electrodes and are connected by a conducting wire.
    • Two solutions are connected by salt bridge.
    • The oxidation and reduction half reactions occur at separate electrodes and electric current flows through the wire.

Salt Bridge and its functions

• Salt bridge is inverted U-tube containing solution of inert electrolyte with agar-agar or gelatin to convert into semi solid form.

• Ions of inert electrolyte do not involve in any chemical change.

The electrolyte in salt bridge should be such that speed of its cation is nearly equal to speed of its anion. Ex. KCl, $KNO_3$, $NH_4NO_3$

• If $Ag^+$, $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$,$\text{Pb}^{2+}$, $\text{Tl}^+$ ions are present in a cell then KCl is not used because there can be formation of precipitate of AgCl, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ $\text{PbCl}_2$  or TlCl.

Functions

• It connects the solution of two half cells to complete the circuit.
    • It maintains the electrical neutrality of the solution in order to give continuous flow or generation of current.
    • If the salt bridge is removed then voltage drops to zero.
    • It prevents the liquid -liquid junction potential. The potential difference which arises between two solutions when they are brought in contact with each other.

Cell Representation:

$\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{ZnSO}_4(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{CuSO}_4(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Cu(s)}$

Anode                        II                Cathode

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Nernst Equation:

  • Relates the cell potential to its standard electrode potential and reaction quotient(Q).
  • Essential for understanding electrochemical cells under non-standard conditions.
Cell EMF (Electromotive Force):

  • The potential difference between two electrodes in an electrochemical cell.
  • Determines the cell's ability to drive an electric current.

blocks.title: Applications of Nernst Equation and Golden key point
blocks.text:
Applications of Nernst Equation:

• Calculation of electrode potential (ERP or EOP)
    • Calculation of electrode potential and pH or hydrogen electrode
    • Calculation of EMF of cell ($E_{cell}$)

• Prediction and feasibility of a cell reaction
    • Calculation of equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) and $\Delta G^\circ $

Golden Key Point:

• The value of electrode potential does not depend on stoichiometry of half reactions as it is an intensive property.
    • Gibb's free energy is an extensive property.
    • In an electrolytic cell, cathode is negative terminal whereas in Galvanic cell cathode is a positive terminal.
    • Cell reaction is spontaneous, if

$\Delta G$ = – ve        or      $E_{\text{cell}} = +\text{ve}$

• Cell reaction will be in equilibrium, if

$\Delta G$ = 0           or     $-nFE_{\text{cell}}  $= 0 or $E_{\text{cell}} $ = 0

• Work done by a cell:

Let 'n' faraday charge be taken out of a cell of EMF 'E' ; then work done by the cell will be calculated as:

Work = Charge × Potential = nF × E

Work done by cell = Decrease in free energy

-$\Delta G = -nFE \quad \text{or} \quad W_{\text{max}} = +nFE^\circ$

where E° is standard EMF of the cell.

Cell reaction

$0.30 - \frac{0.059}{6} \log \frac{[0.1]^2}{[0.01]^3} = 0.30 + \frac{0.24}{6} = 0.34 \, \text{V}$

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Conductance (G)

$G=\frac{1}{R}$

Explanation: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in Siemens.

• Specific resistance/Resistivity ($\rho$)

$R = \rho l/\ A$

$\ell = 1\ \text{cm}, \ A = 1\ \text{cm}^2, \ \text{therefore} \ \rho = R$

$\therefore V = A \times \ell = 1\ \text{cm}^3$

$\text{Unit of } \rho \rightarrow \Omega \cdot \text{cm}$

• Specific conductance/ Conductivity (k(kappa) :-

It is defined as the reciprocal of specific resistance,

$ k = \frac{1}{\rho} $

𝜅 = 𝐺 × 𝐺*

Specific conductance = Conductance × Cell constant

Hence specific conductivity of a solution is defined as the conductance offered by 1 $cm^3$of electrolytic solution.

$\ \text{Unit of } k = \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}\ (S × \text{cm}^{-1})$

• Cell constant

G*= l/A

• Molar conductivity or Molar conductance
 $(\Lambda_m \text{ or } \lambda_m)$

$\Lambda_m = k \times V$

$\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$

$\text{Unit} \rightarrow \Omega^{-1} \, \text{cm}^2 \, \text{mol}^{-1}$($ \text{S } \text{cm}^2 \, \text{mol}^{-1}$)

• Relation between $\Lambda_{\text{eq}} \quad \text{and} \quad \Lambda_m$

$\Lambda_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\Lambda_m}{V_f}$

Debye Huckel Onsager equation

 \quad \text{}$$$

blocks.text:
Standard Electrode Potential ($E^\circ$):

  • Tendency of a chemical species to be reduced, measured under standard conditions.
  • Formula: $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ=E_{\text{cathode}}^\circ-E_{\text{anode}}^\circ$  in reduction potential

blocks.title: Nernst Equation
blocks.text:
It gives relation between electrode potential/ EMF of cell and concentration of electrolytic solution. Walther Nernst derived a relation between free energy change  $ \Delta G^\circ $ and Reaction quotient (Q).

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT \ln Q$

where   $\Delta G$ and $ \Delta G^\circ $are free energy change and standard free energy change; ‘Q’ is reaction quotient.

$-\Delta G = nFE$;  $-\Delta G^\circ = nFE^\circ$

blocks.title: Formulas and mathematics relations
blocks.text:
Nernst Equation:

$E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF} \ln Q$

where, $E$: Cell potential under non-standard conditions

$E^\circ$: Standard cell potential

$R$: Universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K)

$T$: Temperature in Kelvin

$n$: Number of moles of electrons transferred

$F$: Faraday's constant (96485 C/mol)

$Q$: Reaction quotient

Simplified at 25°C (298 K):

$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$

$E = E_0 - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log \frac{[P]}{[R]}$

In general, for a redox cell reaction involving the transfer of n electrons

$aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$

$E_{\text{Cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:

$W = Z.Q$

$\mathrm{W}=\frac{\mathrm{E} . \mathrm{I} . \mathrm{t}}{96500}$

$\mathrm{E}=\frac{\text { mol. } \mathrm{wt}}{\mathrm{n}-\text { factor }}$

Variables:

$W$ : mass of substance deposited (in gm)

$Q$ : total charge passed = I × t

Z : Electrochemical equivalent

E : Equivalent weight

I : Current (in Ampere )

t : time (in second)

96500 : Faraday's constant F

Assumptions: Simple ionic substances, 100% efficiency.

  • Faraday's Second Law:
$\mathrm{W}=\frac{\mathrm{E} . \mathrm{I} . \mathrm{t}}{96500}$

if I and t is contant(Constant current for same time) then

W ∝ E

$\frac{W_1}{E_1} = \frac{W_2}{E_2}$
